records.transcript:
Dear Requester

Thank you for your email. As the main contact for Freedom of Information, I have not seen your request previously but I will explain what I can in regards to your original request:

I am writing to enquire whether any records or references are held in relation to the following historical deaths that occurred in the Cardiff & Vale / Llandough area:

1. William (Billy) Buckler
   - Died at Llandough Hospital on or about 29 May 1990, aged 41
   - Reported cause: heart attack

2. Mary Doreen Williams
   - Born 10 August 1913
   - Death registered March 1983, South Glamorgan (Vol 28, Page 3029)

Although these pre-date the current Medical Examiner Service, I would be grateful if you could advise whether any legacy records, referrals, or related documentation exist, or direct me to the appropriate archive or department that may hold such information.

The All Wales Medical Examiner Service was introduced on a non-statutory basis in 2019. It operated across Wales to provide independent scrutiny of deaths that were not referred to a coroner so deaths in 1983 and 1990 would not apply in this case. The service became statutory on 9 September 2024, when the death certification reforms came into force in England and Wales. From that date, independent scrutiny by a Medical Examiner became a legal requirement before registration of all non-coronial deaths. Therefore, for deaths in 1983/1990, there would have been no Medical Examiner Service. Death certification would have been carried out by the attending doctor, with referrals made to the coroner where required under the rules that existed at the time. The Medical Examiner system only arrived many decades later.

If both deaths occurred in Secondary Care, Hospitals do maintain records of deaths that occurred in their facilities, but these are not generally public records.

The official legal record of a death is the death certificate registered with the local registrar and held by the General Register Office (GRO). In Wales, you can obtain copies of death certificates dating back before 1983 if the death was registered.  Hospital medical records are usually retained under NHS records management policies and may still exist for deaths in 1983, but access is restricted because they contain confidential medical information.

If you are researching a specific death from 1990 at Llandough Hospital, possible sources are:


  1.  Death certificate from the General Register Office.
  2.  Glamorgan Archives for historical NHS administrative records.
  3.  The relevant NHS body that inherited Llandough Hospital records, now part of Cardiff and Vale University Health Board.
  4.  Coroner's records, if an inquest was held.

In 1990, Llandough Hospital was still an NHS hospital managed through the local health authority system. This was under the South Glamorgan Health Authority, which was responsible for hospitals in the Cardiff and Vale area before NHS trusts were created in the early 1990s and now the Cardiff & Vale University Health Board.

They can be contacted here:

Health Records - Cardiff and Vale University Health Board<https://cavuhb.nhs.wales/our-services/health-records/>

GP records are generally retained for a long period. Under current NHS records management guidance, GP records are typically kept for 10 years after a patient's death before being destroyed so these records would be out of scope.

I have asked our registration team to search both patients and there are no records found for either patients due to the time elapsed.

Further comments have been provided below in red for reference.

I hope that this is an acceptable response.

Yours sincerely,

Tim Knifton, MSc Gwybodeg Iechyd/Health Informatics
Rheolwr Rheoli Gwybodaeth/Information Governance Manager
Partneriaeth Cydwasanaethau GIG Cymru/NHS Wales Shared Services Partnership

Michelle,

Thanks for your prompt response.

I'd like to request an internal review of the handling of my enquiry and, insofar as it constitutes a Freedom of Information request, of the conclusion that no relevant records are held.

I am not challenging the conclusion simply because it is inconvenient to my enquiry. Rather, I would like to establish whether an adequate search was undertaken before the conclusion was reached.

Your latest response states that the Medical Examiner Service would not hold “any records whatsoever” or have “any knowledge” of these patients. Given that the deaths occurred in 1983 and 1990, before the establishment of the current Medical Examiner Service, I would be grateful if the internal review could specifically establish whether the search extended beyond current Medical Examiner records to any relevant predecessor, legacy or transferred records. This would have not been something that the medical examiner would have been able to complete as explained above.

In particular, could the review please confirm:

  1.  What records and information systems were searched; primary care registration system
  2.  Whether any legacy or predecessor records relating to the medical examination or certification of deaths were considered; No legacy records going back to 1983/1990 would be considered as the service concentrates on independent scrutiny of deaths that were not referred to a coroner in the present day
  3.  Whether records relating to Llandough Hospital, where William Buckler is recorded as having died in approximately May 1990, are held by the Medical Examiner Service, NHS Wales Shared Services Partnership, another NHS body, or an archive to which you have access or knowledge; As explained above
  4.  Whether any records concerning referrals to a coroner, inquests, post-mortems or other investigations into these deaths would have been held separately from Medical Examiner records;
  5.  Whether the possibility of records having been transferred to an archive or successor organisation was considered; This would have been completed under the old Health Authority and retained for the specific time period under records management policies.
  6.  Whether the statement that no records are held means that no relevant records are held by the South Wales Central Medical Examiner Service specifically, or that searches have established that no such records are held anywhere within NHS Wales Shared Services Partnership; and Medical Examiner was not established until 2019, historic records going back to the 1980s and 1990s would not form part of the remit of the service.
  7.  If the records are not held by your organisation, whether you can identify the appropriate current custodian or archive for any surviving historical records. Explained above

For clarity, the individuals concerned are:

  *   William (Billy) Buckler – died at Llandough Hospital on or about 29 May 1990, aged 41; and
  *   Mary Doreen Williams – born 10 August 1913; death registered in March 1983, South Glamorgan, Vol. 28, p. 3029.

I would be grateful if this could be treated as a formal internal review rather than simply a further general enquiry.

I would also ask that the review be undertaken by someone who was not responsible for the original response, where practicable.

My purpose is to establish a reliable documentary record and, in particular, to distinguish between:

(a) records which do not exist;

(b) records which once existed but have been destroyed;

(c) records which exist but are held by another organisation; and

(d) records which are held within NHS Wales or a predecessor organisation but were not identified by the original search.

I would be grateful for confirmation of the review and, where applicable, the relevant FOI reference number.

Kind regards,

Requester

records.transcript:
Mr Knifton,

Very good of you. Thank you for your detailed response and for taking the
time to clarify the position. I have passed my concerned to the National
Crime Agency too.

I appreciate the confirmation that the All Wales Medical Examiner Service
did not exist at the time of either death and that, consequently, it would
not hold predecessor records relating to deaths in 1983 or 1990.

I am also grateful that you asked the registration team to conduct a search
and confirmed that no records were found for either individual on the
systems searched.

For the purposes of maintaining an accurate documentary record, I would be
grateful if you could clarify one final point. My objective is to
distinguish clearly between records which were never held by the present
organisation, records which once existed but have since been destroyed, and
records which may survive with a successor body or archive.

As I understand your response, the position is as follows:

   - the Medical Examiner Service holds no relevant historical records
   because the service was not established until 2019;
   - the primary care registration system and the records searched by your
   registration team contain no records for either William Buckler or Mary
   Doreen Williams;
   - any original hospital or health-authority records relating to these
   deaths would have fallen under the former South Glamorgan Health Authority
   and its applicable records-management arrangements;
   - surviving hospital records relating to William Buckler's death at
   Llandough Hospital may therefore be held by, or have passed to, Cardiff and
   Vale University Health Board or another successor/archive repository;
   - records relating to any coroner referral, post-mortem or inquest, if
   such events occurred, may have been held separately; and
   - GP records may have been destroyed under applicable retention
   arrangements, although the present search has not identified a specific
   destruction record for either individual.

If that is an accurate summary of your position, no further action is
required from your office. I would simply be grateful for confirmation,
particularly that the statement that no records were found does not amount
to confirmation that no historical records ever existed elsewhere within
the former South Glamorgan Health Authority system.

Thank you again for clarifying the historical position and for identifying
Cardiff and Vale University Health Board, Glamorgan Archives and the
coroner's records as the more appropriate avenues for further enquiry.

Kind regards,

*Requester *
**

Thank you for your email. As the main contact for Freedom of Information, I have not seen your request previously but I will explain what I can in regards to your original request:

I am writing to enquire whether any records or references are held in relation to the following historical deaths that occurred in the Cardiff & Vale / Llandough area:

   - Died at Llandough Hospital on or about 29 May 1990, aged 41

   - Born 10 August 1913
   - Death registered March 1983, South Glamorgan (Vol 28, Page 3029)

Although these pre-date the current Medical Examiner Service, I would be grateful if you could advise whether any legacy records, referrals, or related documentation exist, or direct me to the appropriate archive or department that may hold such information.

The All Wales Medical Examiner Service was introduced on a non-statutory basis in 2019. It operated across Wales to provide independent scrutiny of deaths that were not referred to a coroner so deaths in 1983 and 1990 would not apply in this case. The service became statutory on 9 September 2024, when the death certification reforms came into force in England and Wales. From that date, independent scrutiny by a Medical Examiner became a legal requirement before registration of all non-coronial deaths. Therefore, for deaths in 1983/1990, there would have been no Medical Examiner Service. Death certification would have been carried out by the attending doctor, with referrals made to the coroner where required under the rules that existed at the time. The Medical Examiner system only arrived many decades later.

If both deaths occurred in Secondary Care, Hospitals do maintain records of deaths that occurred in their facilities, but these are not generally public records.

The official legal record of a death is the death certificate registered with the local registrar and held by the General Register Office (GRO). In Wales, you can obtain copies of death certificates dating back before 1983 if the death was registered.  Hospital medical records are usually retained under NHS records management policies and may still exist for deaths in 1983, but access is restricted because they contain confidential medical information.

If you are researching a specific death from 1990 at Llandough Hospital, possible sources are:


  1.  Death certificate from the General Register Office.
  2.  Glamorgan Archives for historical NHS administrative records.
  3.  The relevant NHS body that inherited Llandough Hospital records, now part of Cardiff and Vale University Health Board.
  4.  Coroner's records, if an inquest was held.

In 1990, Llandough Hospital was still an NHS hospital managed through the local health authority system. This was under the South Glamorgan Health Authority, which was responsible for hospitals in the Cardiff and Vale area before NHS trusts were created in the early 1990s and now the Cardiff & Vale University Health Board.

They can be contacted here:

Health Records - Cardiff and Vale University Health Board 

GP records are generally retained for a long period. Under current NHS records management guidance, GP records are typically kept for 10 years after a patient's death before being destroyed so these records would be out of scope.

I have asked our registration team to search both patients and there are no records found for either patients due to the time elapsed.

The All Wales Medical Examiner Service was introduced on a non-statutory basis in 2019. It operated across Wales to provide independent scrutiny of deaths that were not referred to a coroner so deaths in 1983 and 1990 would not apply in this case. The service became statutory on 9 September 2024, when the death certification reforms came into force in England and Wales. From that date, independent scrutiny by a Medical Examiner became a legal requirement before registration of all non-coronial deaths. Therefore, for deaths in 1983/1990, there would have been no Medical Examiner Service. Death certification would have been carried out by the attending doctor, with referrals made to the coroner where required under the rules that existed at the time. The Medical Examiner system only arrived many decades later.

If both deaths occurred in Secondary Care, Hospitals do maintain records of deaths that occurred in their facilities, but these are not generally public records.

The official legal record of a death is the death certificate registered with the local registrar and held by the General Register Office (GRO). In Wales, you can obtain copies of death certificates dating back before 1983 if the death was registered.  Hospital medical records are usually retained under NHS records management policies and may still exist for deaths in 1983, but access is restricted because they contain confidential medical information.

If you are researching a specific death from 1990 at Llandough Hospital, possible sources are:


  1.  Death certificate from the General Register Office.
  2.  Glamorgan Archives for historical NHS administrative records.
  3.  The relevant NHS body that inherited Llandough Hospital records, now part of Cardiff and Vale University Health Board.
  4.  Coroner's records, if an inquest was held.

In 1990, Llandough Hospital was still an NHS hospital managed through the local health authority system. This was under the South Glamorgan Health Authority, which was responsible for hospitals in the Cardiff and Vale area before NHS trusts were created in the early 1990s and now the Cardiff & Vale University Health Board.

They can be contacted here:

Health Records - Cardiff and Vale University Health Board 

GP records are generally retained for a long period. Under current NHS records management guidance, GP records are typically kept for 10 years after a patient's death before being destroyed so these records would be out of scope.

I have asked our registration team to search both patients and there are no records found for either patients due to the time elapsed.

The All Wales Medical Examiner Service was introduced on a non-statutory basis in 2019. It operated across Wales to provide independent scrutiny of deaths that were not referred to a coroner so deaths in 1983 and 1990 would not apply in this case. The service became statutory on 9 September 2024, when the death certification reforms came into force in England and Wales. From that date, independent scrutiny by a Medical Examiner became a legal requirement before registration of all non-coronial deaths. Therefore, for deaths in 1983/1990, there would have been no Medical Examiner Service. Death certification would have been carried out by the attending doctor, with referrals made to the coroner where required under the rules that existed at the time. The Medical Examiner system only arrived many decades later.



If both deaths occurred in Secondary Care, Hospitals do maintain records of deaths that occurred in their facilities, but these are not generally public records.



The official legal record of a death is the death certificate registered with the local registrar and held by the General Register Office (GRO). In Wales, you can obtain copies of death certificates dating back before 1983 if the death was registered.  Hospital medical records are usually retained under NHS records management policies and may still exist for deaths in 1983, but access is restricted because they contain confidential medical information.



If you are researching a specific death from 1990 at Llandough Hospital, possible sources are:



  1.  Death certificate from the General Register Office.
  2.  Glamorgan Archives for historical NHS administrative records.
  3.  The relevant NHS body that inherited Llandough Hospital records, now part of Cardiff and Vale University Health Board.
  4.  Coroner's records, if an inquest was held.



In 1990, Llandough Hospital was still an NHS hospital managed through the local health authority system. This was under the South Glamorgan Health Authority, which was responsible for hospitals in the Cardiff and Vale area before NHS trusts were created in the early 1990s and now the Cardiff & Vale University Health Board.



They can be contacted here:

GP records are generally retained for a long period. Under current NHS records management guidance, GP records are typically kept for 10 years after a patient's death before being destroyed so these records would be out of scope.

Thank you for your request for information received on 27 July 2026 concerning records relating to a reported discovery at Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough, including a soldier, horse remains and items described as a visor and lance.

Amgueddfa Cymru has undertaken searches of its collections management systems, accession records and associated documentation.

We have not identified any records relating to the acquisition, accession, donation, transfer or deposit of a medieval visor, lance, helmet or other item of armour associated with Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough. We have also not identified records relating to the specific discovery described in your request, including records of associated human or animal remains, reburial records, excavation reports, watching briefs or discovery reports.

Accordingly, under section 1(1)(a) of the Freedom of Information Act 2000, our response is that Amgueddfa Cymru does not hold the requested information.

For completeness, our searches identified records relating to other archaeological finds from Church Farm, Llandough and to other archaeological discoveries recorded at Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough. These records do not relate to, nor are they otherwise associated with, the discovery described in your request. We have therefore not considered them to fall within the scope of this request.

If you are dissatisfied with this response, you may request an internal review by writing to [email redacted]<[email redacted]> within 40 working days of the date of this letter.

To: Coroner Admin <[email redacted]>
Subject: Re: FOI / Records Request – Deaths of William (Billy) Buckler (1990) and Mary Doreen Williams (1983)


Dear Bev,

Thank you for checking the system and for your prompt and helpful reply.

I am grateful for the clarification regarding the historical position of Cardiff and Vale cases prior to 2002, and I will now pursue enquiries with Glamorgan Archives.

Before I do so, I would be grateful if I could clarify one point concerning the result of your search, particularly in relation to my grandmother, Mary Doreen Williams.

My purpose is not simply genealogical. I am attempting to reconstruct and forensically assess the historical circumstances surrounding her death in 1983, and there is information concerning the circumstances before and around her death which I am seeking to reconcile against the surviving official documentary record.

Could you therefore please confirm whether your statement that you are "unable to locate any details" means only that neither individual appears in the records or computerised/indexed system currently available to your office, or whether your office is able positively to state that neither death was ever referred to the coroner?

In particular, if you are able to clarify, I would be grateful to know whether the absence of a record in your system excludes, or does not exclude, the historical existence of:

  *   a report of the death to a coroner;
  *   a preliminary coroner's enquiry;
  *   a post-mortem examination;
  *   an inquest;
  *   correspondence with the police, hospital or other authority;
  *   a case file or register subsequently transferred to an archive or destroyed in accordance with an applicable retention policy.

I appreciate that you may not hold the historical records themselves. I am not asking you to speculate about the circumstances of either death. I am simply seeking to ensure that I correctly understand the evidential significance of the negative search result before proceeding to the archive.

If possible, I would also be grateful if you could confirm the name of the coroner jurisdiction or office responsible for Llandough/Llandough Hospital in March 1983, when Mary Doreen Williams died, and whether you know which body would have inherited or transferred that jurisdiction's surviving records.

For completeness, if there are any records held off-system, legacy indexes, paper registers, accession records or transfer information which are not searchable through the system you checked, I would be grateful if you could let me know whether those exist and who now holds them.

I appreciate your assistance. I am trying to establish the documentary facts carefully and avoid drawing conclusions before the relevant records have been located or ruled out.

Kind regards,

Requester

Bev,

Thank you for clarifying the position regarding the Freedom of Information Act.

I understand that coroners and their records are not subject to the FOI access regime. I am therefore not seeking to pursue the matter as an FOI request if that is not the appropriate route.

My primary purpose is to establish whether either of these deaths was ever referred to the coroner and, if so, whether any surviving record exists and what lawful route is available for an interested family member to obtain information from it.

I would therefore be grateful if you could clarify the following, insofar as you are able:

  1.  Whether your office has any record or index indicating that either William (Billy) Buckler, who died at Llandough Hospital on or about 29 May 1990, or Mary Doreen Williams, whose death was registered in March 1983 in South Glamorgan (Vol. 28, p. 3029), was reported to or dealt with by the coroner;
  2.  If either death was the subject of a coroner's investigation, whether an inquest, post-mortem examination or other coroner's investigation took place;
  3.  Whether any historical record relating to either death remains in the custody of the coroner's service, or whether such records have been transferred to another archive, authority or successor body;
  4.  If records exist but cannot be disclosed directly, what procedure is available for a descendant or other interested person to establish the basic factual information concerning the case;
  5.  If your office has no record whatsoever of either death, whether that means that no coroner's record exists, or simply that the surviving records are no longer held by your office.

I am particularly interested in establishing the documentary chain rather than necessarily seeking disclosure of confidential medical information. A confirmation that a death was, or was not, referred to the coroner would itself be useful.

If you are not the appropriate office to answer these historical-record questions, I would be grateful if you could identify the relevant archive, successor body or other custodian to whom I should direct the enquiry.

Thank you again for your assistance.

Regards,



Requester

Thank you for your e-mail dated 20/08/2026.

Although appointed and paid for by local councils, the coroner is not a local government officer but holds office under the Crown.

Coroners are not designated as public authorities under the Freedom of Information Act 2000 and therefore their records are not subject to the information access regime of this Act.

Please let me know if I can be of further assistance.

BP Archive Team,

I am writing to enquire about records held within the BP corporate archive relating to the former Great House Farm / Ty Mawr property at Llandough, near Penarth, Glamorgan, South Wales.

I am conducting historical and legal research into the property, which was acquired by BP Pension Trust Ltd in December 1969 and subsequently administered by BP Properties Ltd. The property was the subject of extensive litigation, including BP Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987] EWCA Civ 2, followed by the eviction of the occupying family in 1988 and demolition of the farmhouse later that year.

Research context

The central issue of my research is the identification of the individual parcels comprising the historic property.

The evidence currently being examined indicates that the historic complex may have comprised separately identifiable:

  *   a house-and-garden plot;
  *   a western agricultural/farm plot containing the barn, stables and courtyard; and
  *   an eastern cottages plot.

Later mapping and Land Registry records appear to have treated some of these areas as a combined property.

I am therefore particularly interested in establishing what BP itself understood the boundaries and constituent parcels of the property to be, and when any change or consolidation of those parcels occurred.

Records sought

I would be grateful if the BP Archive could search its holdings for records concerning:

  *   BP Properties Ltd;
  *   BP Pension Trust Ltd;
  *   British Petroleum and relevant predecessor/subsidiary property records;
  *   Great House Farm / Great House / Ty Mawr, Llandough;
  *   Llandough-juxta-Penarth / Cogan / Penarth;
  *   the Williams and Buckler families;
  *   possession proceedings and enforcement, particularly 1955, 1962 and 1974-1988;
  *   property acquisition, title investigation and disposal;
  *   conveyances, title deeds, abstracts of title and schedules of deeds;
  *   estate-management correspondence;
  *   property, site and boundary plans;
  *   Land Registry correspondence and registration, particularly 1982-1983.

The relevant period is approximately 1955-1988, with particular emphasis on 1962-1983.

Three priority categories

If relevant material survives, I would particularly like to identify the following, in this order:

1. The BP Properties Ltd / BP Pension Trust Ltd property file for Great House Farm / Ty Mawr, Llandough

In particular, any acquisition/title file containing the original property description, conveyances, title investigation, schedules of deeds, property plans, boundary plans or correspondence identifying exactly which land and buildings BP considered to form the property.

2. The legal/property file relating to the 1962 possession proceedings and subsequent enforcement/re-entry

In particular, any BP legal correspondence, instructions to solicitors, plans, property descriptions or internal documents identifying the land and buildings to which the possession order was understood to apply.

3. The 1982-1983 title/registration/consolidation file

In particular, correspondence, plans, conveyances, title investigation and Land Registry material concerning the registration or amalgamation of the relevant parcels, including any documentation showing how the house-and-garden, eastern cottages and western farm/barn/stables/courtyard areas were treated.

If these exact files do not survive, I would be very grateful for the nearest surviving files, alternative references or catalogue entries covering the same transactions.

Access

I would also appreciate advice on:

  *   whether the relevant records are available for public research;
  *   whether they can be viewed in person at the BP Archive at the University of Warwick;
  *   whether advance appointment or reader registration is required;
  *   whether particular records require advance retrieval;
  *   whether copies or digital reproductions can be ordered; and
  *   whether any relevant records are subject to closure or other access restrictions.

I am happy to provide further information, including the relevant court case reference, property names, dates and Land Registry title numbers, if this would assist the archivist in identifying the records.

Research purpose

I am particularly interested in contemporary BP documentation rather than later summaries, because the central research question is what BP itself understood the property's legal identity, boundaries and constituent parcels to be at the relevant dates.

Thank you very much for any assistance you can provide.

Yours sincerely,

Requester

Dear FOI Team,

Thank you for your response.

I am requesting an internal review of the handling of my request. I do not
consider the response sufficient because it appears that the searches were
conducted too narrowly around the later description of a "medieval visor,
lance, helmet or other item of armour", rather than around the underlying
historical discovery at Great House Farm itself.

The issue I am investigating is a reported nineteenth-century discovery at
Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough. My understanding from contemporary
or near-contemporary newspaper and historical accounts is that the
discovery was described as involving the remains of a Roman soldier, with
associated remains and objects. The dating and description of the
individual objects as "medieval" may therefore itself be inaccurate, or may
represent a later conflation or retelling of the original discovery.

Your response is particularly significant because it states:

«"Our searches identified records relating to ... other archaeological
discoveries recorded at Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough. These
records do not relate to, nor are they otherwise associated with, the
discovery described in your request. We have therefore not considered them
to fall within the scope of this request."»

I respectfully challenge that approach.

The central question is precisely whether the discovery described in later
historical accounts can be identified, corroborated, corrected or explained
through the Museum's records concerning archaeological discoveries at Great
House Farm. If the Museum has identified records relating to other
discoveries at the same historically significant site, it is not sufficient
simply to conclude internally that they are unrelated without disclosing
what those discoveries are, when they were recorded, and the basis upon
which that conclusion was reached.

I therefore request that the internal review reconsider the scope of my
request and undertake searches using, at minimum, the following terms and
concepts:

- Great House Farm
- Ty Mawr
- Llandough
- Llandough, Cardiff
- Roman soldier
- Roman burial
- Roman grave
- Roman remains
- human remains
- skeleton
- horse remains
- equine remains
- soldier and horse
- cavalry burial
- military burial
- grave goods
- Roman military equipment
- visor
- helmet
- lance
- spear
- armour
- archaeological discovery
- nineteenth-century discovery
- 1870 and adjacent years

Please also search for relevant records under alternative historical
place-name indexing, donor names, findspot descriptions, parish names and
catalogue terminology where the precise modern name "Great House Farm" may
not have been used.

Most importantly, I ask that you disclose sufficient information about the
"other archaeological discoveries" which your searches identified at Great
House Farm to enable me to understand and assess the Museum's conclusion
that they are unrelated. This should include, so far as held:

1. A description or title of each relevant discovery or record.
2. The approximate date of the discovery or record.
3. The nature of the material or remains involved.
4. Any accession number, catalogue number or archival reference.
5. The recorded provenance or findspot.
6. Any dating attributed to the discovery.
7. The basis upon which Amgueddfa Cymru concluded that each record was
unrelated to the nineteenth-century discovery described in my request.

I am not asking the Museum to create new archaeological opinions or
undertake speculative research. I am asking for recorded information which
has already been identified during the searches and which directly concerns
archaeological discoveries at the specific site named in my request.

If the Museum maintains that any of those records fall outside the original
scope, then please treat this email additionally as a refined request for
the recorded information identified above.

I would also ask the reviewer to consider whether the original response
gave insufficient weight to the possibility that the historical account may
have inaccurately dated or described the find. A search which excludes
Roman, nineteenth-century, burial and equine terminology risks missing the
very records capable of establishing what was actually discovered beneath
Great House Farm.

Given that your searches have already identified records concerning
archaeological discoveries at Great House Farm itself, I would be grateful
for a full reconsideration and disclosure of the recorded information
requested above.

Yours faithfully,

Requester

Dear FOI Team,

I am requesting an internal review of the handling of my request. I do not consider the response sufficient because it appears that the searches were conducted too narrowly around the later description of a "medieval visor, lance, helmet or other item of armour", rather than around the underlying historical discovery at Great House Farm itself.

The issue I am investigating is a reported nineteenth-century discovery at Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough. My understanding from contemporary or near-contemporary newspaper and historical accounts is that the discovery was described as involving the remains of a Roman soldier, with associated remains and objects. The dating and description of the individual objects as "medieval" may therefore itself be inaccurate, or may represent a later conflation or retelling of the original discovery.

Your response is particularly significant because it states:

<"Our searches identified records relating to ... other archaeological discoveries recorded at Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough. These records do not relate to, nor are they otherwise associated with, the discovery described in your request. We have therefore not considered them to fall within the scope of this request.">

I respectfully challenge that approach.

The central question is precisely whether the discovery described in later historical accounts can be identified, corroborated, corrected or explained through the Museum's records concerning archaeological discoveries at Great House Farm. If the Museum has identified records relating to other discoveries at the same historically significant site, it is not sufficient simply to conclude internally that they are unrelated without disclosing what those discoveries are, when they were recorded, and the basis upon which that conclusion was reached.

I therefore request that the internal review reconsider the scope of my request and undertake searches using, at minimum, the following terms and concepts:

- Great House Farm
- Ty Mawr
- Llandough
- Llandough, Cardiff
- Roman soldier
- Roman burial
- Roman grave
- Roman remains
- human remains
- skeleton
- horse remains
- equine remains
- soldier and horse
- cavalry burial
- military burial
- grave goods
- Roman military equipment
- visor
- helmet
- lance
- spear
- armour
- archaeological discovery
- nineteenth-century discovery
- 1870 and adjacent years

Please also search for relevant records under alternative historical place-name indexing, donor names, findspot descriptions, parish names and catalogue terminology where the precise modern name "Great House Farm" may not have been used.

Most importantly, I ask that you disclose sufficient information about the "other archaeological discoveries" which your searches identified at Great House Farm to enable me to understand and assess the Museum's conclusion that they are unrelated. This should include, so far as held:

1. A description or title of each relevant discovery or record.
2. The approximate date of the discovery or record.
3. The nature of the material or remains involved.
4. Any accession number, catalogue number or archival reference.
5. The recorded provenance or findspot.
6. Any dating attributed to the discovery.
7. The basis upon which Amgueddfa Cymru concluded that each record was unrelated to the nineteenth-century discovery described in my request.

I am not asking the Museum to create new archaeological opinions or undertake speculative research. I am asking for recorded information which has already been identified during the searches and which directly concerns archaeological discoveries at the specific site named in my request.

If the Museum maintains that any of those records fall outside the original scope, then please treat this email additionally as a refined request for the recorded information identified above.

I would also ask the reviewer to consider whether the original response gave insufficient weight to the possibility that the historical account may have inaccurately dated or described the find. A search which excludes Roman, nineteenth-century, burial and equine terminology risks missing the very records capable of establishing what was actually discovered beneath Great House Farm.

Given that your searches have already identified records concerning archaeological discoveries at Great House Farm itself, I would be grateful for a full reconsideration and disclosure of the recorded information requested above.

Yours faithfully,

Requester

Bev,

Thank you for the clarification. The distinction is important to my enquiry.

I am conducting a forensic reconstruction of the historical circumstances
surrounding the *BP Properties Ltd v Buckler* dispute, including the events
surrounding Mary Doreen Williams, and her death in March 1983.

Mary died during the very short period in which she would have had an
opportunity to challenge the registration of her land in BP’s name. Her
ownership claim was never adjudicated or exstinguished. BP's award of
possession of her land (not ownership) resulted in a brutal dispossession
of her children and grandchildren resulting in a ECHR case in 1989, which
also prioritised BP's rights over the families.

I am therefore examining the documentary evidence concerning both the
land-registration dispute and the circumstances surrounding her death. I am
not suggesting from the timing alone that the two matters were connected;
rather, I am seeking to establish the underlying facts and ensure that the
surviving official record has been properly accounted for.

For that reason, I need to distinguish between *a historical absence of a
coronial record* and *the absence of a record from a modern computer system
which does not contain that historical material*.

I understand from your latest email that your computer system does not
store information concerning referrals received in 1983 or before. On that
basis, I understand that the search of your present system cannot establish
whether Mary Doreen Williams was or was not referred to the coroner.

Could I therefore clarify two points separately?

*1. Mary Doreen Williams — March 1983*

Does your office have any information concerning where the historical
records of the coroner responsible for Llandough Hospital in March 1983 are
now held, even if those records are no longer searchable by your office?

I am trying to establish the documentary chain:

*responsible coroner/jurisdiction → historical registers or case files →
transfer to archive or successor authority → present custodian, or
documented destruction/retention history.*

If you do not know the name of the coroner, could you identify the former
coroner’s jurisdiction or office responsible for Llandough Hospital at that
time? That would enable me to make a properly targeted request to the
relevant archive or records custodian.

You previously indicated that Glamorgan Archives may hold paper copies of
reports and post-mortem examination details. Could you clarify whether you
know that the historical Cardiff and Vale coronial records were actually
transferred to Glamorgan Archives, or whether Glamorgan Archives is being
suggested simply as the most likely repository?

If there is a known archive series, accession, register, transfer record or
other indication of where the former coroner’s records were deposited, that
information would be particularly helpful.

*2. William (Billy) Buckler — May 1990*

There is a separate point concerning William (Billy) Buckler, who died in
1990.

Your latest clarification refers specifically to information for referrals
received in *1983 or before*. As Billy died in 1990, could you please
clarify whether his case was capable of being searched in the computer
system you checked?

If it was searchable, I would be grateful if you could explain what the
negative result means — for example, whether no electronic record exists,
or whether the relevant Cardiff and Vale coronial records for that period
are held elsewhere.

Your earlier email stated:

“Cardiff and Vale cases prior to 2002 should be with the Glamorgan
Archivist.”

Could you please confirm whether that applies to Billy’s 1990 case as well?

More generally, I am trying to establish whether either death generated,
and whether there may now survive:

   - a referral to the coroner;
   - a coroner’s register entry or index;
   - a preliminary investigation or enquiry;
   - a post-mortem examination;
   - an inquest;
   - police, hospital or other official correspondence;
   - cause-of-death documentation;
   - coroner’s case papers; or
   - an archival transfer, retention or destruction record.

I appreciate that some underlying records may be subject to access
restrictions, and I am not asking your office to disclose confidential
medical information at this stage. My immediate objective is more
fundamental: *to establish whether a coronial record was created, whether
it survives, and what happened to it.*

That distinction is important to the historical investigation. A
present-day search producing no result is evidentially quite different from
a historical record establishing that no referral, investigation,
post-mortem or inquest ever took place.

I will now approach Glamorgan Archives, but any information you can provide
regarding the former coroner’s jurisdiction, the historical records held by
that jurisdiction, and their subsequent transfer or disposal would allow me
to make that request considerably more precise.

Thank you again for taking the time to clarify the position. Your latest
explanation has been genuinely helpful in establishing the limitations of
the present electronic search, and I appreciate your assistance in
identifying the surviving historical record.

Regards,

Requester

Glamorgan Archives Team,

Further to my email of 22 August 2026 concerning the DBDT collection and
related Bute, Mountjoy and Western Ground Rents material (particularly
Great House Farm / Tŷ Mawr, Llandough), please treat this as an additional
request.




I have attached an image of the land parcel in question, believed to be in
the mislabelled record in question.

**Request: physical examination of DBDT79/1**

Catalogue entry:

Lease (counterpart) of land and premises situate in Pembroke Terrace,
Cardiff, from the Marquess of Bute to Mr John Williams, May 1877 [1
parchment, plan in margin].

Please examine the original document (not the catalogue description alone)
and confirm:

1. Parties and date – Does the original name the Marquess of Bute and Mr
John Williams, and is it dated May 1877?

2. Property description – Exact wording of the land and premises. Does it
expressly locate the property in Pembroke Terrace, Cardiff?

3. Llandough / other references – Any mention (body text, plan, schedule,
endorsements or annotations) of Llandough, Great House Farm / Tŷ Mawr,
Western Ground Rents, or any locality outside Pembroke Terrace?

4. Marginal plan – Does the plan identify the location sufficiently? If
procedures allow, please supply a digital image or scan of the plan.

5. Further identifying details – Any adjoining owners, plot numbers,
parish, street numbers, measurements, previous ownership, rent,
consideration, or cross-references to other instruments.

If scanning is permitted, images of the parties clause, property
description and marginal plan would be ideal. Otherwise a transcription or
detailed description of those sections will suffice.


**Catalogue wording discrepancy**

Most other 1877 entries in the series describe the grantor as the “Trustees
of the Will of the late Marquess of Bute”. DBDT79/1 is catalogued simply as
“from the Marquess of Bute”.

From the original, please confirm:

- who executed the lease;

- the capacity in which the grantor is described;

- whether the Marquess is shown acting personally or through trustees;

- any evident reason for the difference from the other 1877 entries.

(I note the 3rd Marquess attained majority around this period, but I seek
the Archives’ evidence-based confirmation rather than assumption.)


**Purpose**

I am reconstructing the historical title position for Great House Farm / Tŷ
Mawr, Llandough, and need to distinguish any Cardiff property records from
those relating to the Llandough estate. Please report the physical contents
of DBDT79/1 separately from the catalogue description, noting any
differences.

Thank you for your assistance. I look forward to your response to both the
original enquiry and this request.


Also see attached a letter to my friend earlier today, which puts the
purpose of this enquiry and search and record and its importance into some
context for you. If you're at all interested. It might help you to unearth
records I'm unaware of.

There's 133 houses about to be developed on this land and their title maybe
defective. So please be diligent so that an egregious irreversible mistake
or injustice isn't made.

Regards,


Requester
